name: Mvón-Mvón
overview: The Mvón-Mvón say they have always lived in Yokadouma, where they live alongside the Mbimo, Bayege, Gbaya and Kako. Organised around kinship and a hereditary power exercised by consensus, they live from farming, hunting, fishing and gathering; the labi and the patenge set the rhythm of their ceremonies.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: The group shares the territory with the Mbimo, Bayege, Gbaya and Kako, of comparable demographic weight; each speaks the other's language.
The Mvón-Mvón are now scattered across the towns of Cameroon.
Marriages within the group as well as with neighbours; young people also marry people from other regions.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Original land of the ancestors, which still belongs to them; the group did not come from elsewhere.
The land belongs to God and the ancestors, who bequeathed it to families.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Society is organised around kinship and families that hold land.
Power, hereditary within one family, is exercised at the chiefdom: the chief consults notables, patriarchs and matriarchs and decides by consensus.
Everybody can speak, and the in-laws must be heard.
The former associations in charge of the dead have disappeared with the mortuaries; conflicts are settled through dialogue.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the two families visit each other, and the young woman's family accompanies her to her husband's.
One becomes a man around the age of forty; a young girl becomes a woman around 20. Stated ages: 30 for men, 20 to 25 for women.
Steps: visit to the girl's parents, welcome into her family, marriage proposal, bride price.
Bride price: goats, cooking pots, machetes, blankets; the kola marks recognition and offering.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Formerly, an elder held a worship service to a deity at dawn and at dusk, on hills, near rivers and trees; the group today says it believes in God.
Birth is a joy: the child may be the return of a divine being whose name he takes. Death is the price of faults committed.
Incest is strictly forbidden: the offenders must separate.
A pregnant woman eats neither snake, nor tortoise, nor pork, nor caterpillars (minkón); men and children eat almost everything.
Murder was punished by public beating; today, it is a matter for prison.
Divination by diviners (okán), with cowries, foliage and barks.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, hunting, trade, small livestock. Women: farming, fishing, trade, gathering.
Ancestral crafts for everyday use: bamboo chairs, baskets, mats.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Traditional bark clothing (yete), worn at major ceremonies: ekuán for men, bilat for women, who also wear the wrapper.
Very frequent use of medicinal plants and barks.
Female beauty: hair, calves, face.
Courtship: excellent hunter, good dancer, oratory, beauty, elegance and conduct.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: The labi, an initiatory and funeral dance; the patenge, a festive dance.
Instruments: tam-tam, drum, whistles.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: History, cuisine, clothing and language bring the Mvón-Mvón close to the Mbimo and the Bakando.

sections.title: The names
items: Yaya designates the man, the male relative.
The newborn is often given the name of a deceased member of the family, according to the circumstances.
If a child bearing the name of a forebear dies, that name is considered unlucky and is no longer given.
Nicknames and pseudonyms are in common use.

lessons.title: Who are the Mvón-Mvón? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Mvón-Mvón community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Mvón-Mvón community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Mvón-Mvón community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Mvón-Mvón community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Mvón-Mvón community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Mvón-Mvón call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The group shares the territory with the Mbimo, Bayege, Gbaya and Kako, of comparable demographic weight; each speaks the other's language. • The Mvón-Mvón are now scattered across the towns of Cameroon. • Marriages within the group as well as with neighbours; young people also marry people from other regions. • The original land of the ancestors, which still belongs to them; the group did not come from elsewhere. • The land belongs to God and the ancestors, who bequeathed it to families.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mvón-Mvón say they have always lived in Yokadouma, where they live alongside the Mbimo, Bayege, Gbaya and Kako. Organised around kinship and a hereditary power exercised by consensus, they live from farming, hunting, fishing and gathering; the labi and the patenge set the rhythm of their ceremonies.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Mvón-Mvón community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Mvón-Mvón
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Mvón-Mvón organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Mvón-Mvón village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Mvón-Mvón organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Mvón-Mvón village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Society is organised around kinship and families that hold land. • Power, hereditary within one family, is exercised at the chiefdom: the chief consults notables, patriarchs and matriarchs and decides by consensus. • Everyone may speak, and the in-laws must be heard. • The former associations in charge of the dead have disappeared with the advent of morgues; conflicts are settled through dialogue.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Society is organised around kinship and land-holding families. Power, hereditary within one family, is exercised at the chiefdom: the chief consults notables, patriarchs and matriarchs and decides by consensus. Everyone may speak, and in-laws must be heard.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Mvón-Mvón, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.instruction: In groups: what are the advantages of making decisions by consensus?

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Mvón-Mvón
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Mvón-Mvón, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Mvón-Mvón.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Mvón-Mvón, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Mvón-Mvón.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kouem, kɔkɔ, ngouzok, ngoun (cucumber seed dish), wild mango (ndip). • Drinks: arvi (ripe banana drink). • Men: farming, hunting, trade, small livestock. Women: farming, fishing, trade, gathering.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mvón-Mvón mainly eat kouem, kɔkɔ, ngouzok, ngoun. Traditional drinks: ripe banana drink. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Mvón-Mvón: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Mvón-Mvón
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Mvón-Mvón welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Mvón-Mvón family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Mvón-Mvón welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Mvón-Mvón family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Yaya designates the man, the male relative. • The newborn is often given the name of a deceased family member, according to the circumstances. • If a child who bore the name of an ancestor dies, that name is considered unlucky and is no longer given. • Birth is a joy: the child may be the return of a divine being whose name he takes. Death is the price of faults committed. • One becomes a man around forty; the girl becomes a woman around 20. Stated ages: 30 for the man, 20 to 25 for the woman.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Explain the meaning of three Mvón-Mvón personal names and describe the moment when a child receives its name.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Mvón-Mvón
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments

student.memo: Among the Mvón-Mvón, traditional dances (initiation, funerals, patenge) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum, whistles.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Mvón-Mvón
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mvón-Mvón, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Mvón-Mvón. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mvón-Mvón, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Mvón-Mvón. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, hunting, trade, small livestock. Women: farming, fishing, trade, gathering. • Ancestral crafts for everyday use: bamboo chairs, baskets, mats.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, hunting, trade, small livestock. Women: farming, fishing, trade, gathering. Ancestral crafts for everyday use: bamboo chairs, baskets, mats.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Mvón-Mvón's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I classify

activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Mvón-Mvón
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: serpent, tortue, porc et chenilles pour la femme enceinte

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mvón-Mvón, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Mvón-Mvón. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mvón-Mvón, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Mvón-Mvón. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Formerly, an elder held a worship service to a deity at dawn and at dusk, on hills, near rivers and trees; the group today says it believes in God. • Birth is a joy: the child may be the return of a divine being whose name he or she takes. Death is the price of faults committed. • Incest is strictly forbidden: the offenders must separate. • The pregnant woman eats neither snake, nor tortoise, nor pork, nor caterpillars (minkón); men and children eat almost everything. • Murder was punished by public caning; today, it is a matter for prison.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Formerly, an elder held a worship service to a deity at dawn and at dusk, on hills, near rivers and trees; the group today says it believes in God. Birth is a joy: the child may be the return of a divine being whose name it takes. Death is the price of faults committed.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Mvón-Mvón (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Mvón-Mvón believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Mvón-Mvón
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Mvón-Mvón and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Mvón-Mvón family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Mvón-Mvón greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Mvón-Mvón family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Mvón-Mvón. • Greetings: Udieme = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Udieme / oudieme = morning greeting (one person); Bidieme = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Ngua, Debaleba, Elel, Ena, Eten. • Nicknames and pseudonyms are in common use. • History, cooking, dress and language bring the Mvón-Mvón close to the Mbimo and the Bakando.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Mvón-Mvón are the first steps towards communicating with the Mvón-Mvón. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Mvón-Mvón.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Mvón-Mvón are the first steps towards communicating with the Mvón-Mvón. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
